newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania PM-designate launches economic programme.
newsitem.headline: Romania PM-designate launches economic programme.

text.p: Prime Minister-designate Victor Ciorbea on Monday launched a six-month programme intended to improve living standards and correct economic imbalances.
He will submit the programme to parliament for approval on Tuesday.
"The main target...is to pave a way out of the crisis, check socioeconomic degradation and improve the lives of the people, especially of disadvantaged groups," the draft said.
The programme also aims at speeding up reforms to gain support from international lenders and clear the way for Romania's integration into the NATO and the European Union.
Victor Ciorbea, who became popular as the mayor general of Bucharest, was designated prime minister late last month.
He will head a coalition government including the centrist Democratic Convention bloc -- winners of November's polls -- Social Democrats and representatives of ethnic Hungarians.
Ciorbea and the ministers he designated have yet to win parliamentary approval.
On the social side, the programme pledges to increase child benefits and farmers' pensions, control unemployment and support housing construction.
To ease the hardships of winter, the draft plans to find ways to finance energy imports, while promising to postpone a liberalisation of energy prices until 1998.
Under accords with international financial institutions, Romania is committed to bringing energy prices into line with world market levels.

In a bid to stimulate farm output, the draft aims to complete the distribution of land deeds under a land reform launched five years ago and proposes easing taxation, including cancellation of farm taxes by the year 2000.
Local economists welcomed the draft as a serious commitment to market reforms but said its success depended on the ability to turn guidelines into concrete measures.
The government, mindful of rising inflation and the swollen budget deficit this year, will seek non-inflationary means to cap the budget shortfall.
Inflation this year is estimated at 45 percent, against 27.8 percent in 1995, while the 1996 state budget is expected to post a 4.4 trillion lei deficit.
Relaxed budget policies, higher inflation and upsets in the foreign exchange market led the International Monetary Fund to block credit tranches for Romania earlier this year.
The new government plans to resume talks with the IMF and the World Bank on renewed financing.
Cash-strapped Romania will also work to boost foreign investment, which has reached only $2.0 billion in the past seven years, far less than elsewhere in the region. ($=3,615 lei)
